newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Britain optimistic talks on Cyprus can start.
newsitem.headline: Britain optimistic talks on Cyprus can start.

text.p: Britain expressed hope on Wednesday that Greek and Turkish Cypriots could start direct negotations by June to resolve the long-standing division of the island.
Leaders of the two communities, divided since a Turkish invasion of the northern third of the island in 1974 after a coup sponsored by Athens, have not met since October 1994.

Sir David Hannay, Britain's special envoy for Cyprus, started contacts on the island on Wednesday as the United Nations pushed to get direct negotiations underway after proximity talks, which began on Monday.
Hannay said it was up to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to decide when to conclude the preparatory stage and call the two sides to direct talks.

"Our hope remains that he (the secretary-general) will convene face-to-face negotiations before the end of the first half of 1997," Hannay told reporters after meeting Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.
Later in the afternoon Hannay met with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash for more than an hour at his office in north Nicosia. Hannay refused to divulge details of what was discussed.
"We've agreed that we are not talking to the press...we have covered alot of ground," Hannay said.
Denktash, who heads a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north recognised only by Ankara, described his meeting "useful" but would not give details.
But he said the British envoy had not submitted any proposals.
"We talked of substance and we shall continue to talk of substance...there was an exchange of ideas."
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military ruling in Greece at the time.
Britain, along with Greece and Turkey, is a guarantor power of Cyprus, a former British colony that became independent in 1960.
